title: Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 Rivals OpenAI on Consumer CPUs

tickers.name: Alphabet Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
The newly released 740M parameter multimodal model from Google has quickly become the 4th most liked in the company's history after surpassing EmbeddingGemma 1 in popularity. EmbeddingGemma 2 benchmarks comparably to OpenAI's embedding-3-large and Qwen 8B while running on consumer CPUs rather than GPUs. Though it successfully identified 13 of 14 video clips from a single sentence in testing, it lacks a sense of temporal direction, viewing a video and its reversed version as 99% similar.

Developers have applied the model to build DigUp, an open-source tool for Mac that indexes local files and podcasts. To facilitate on-device search, Google uses Matryoshka embeddings to store only the first 256 of 768 values in a vector. This approach reduces storage needs to 1/3 while maintaining about 95% of the retrieval quality for visuals and speech, according to Google.

selectedTweets.text:
EmbeddingGemma 2 Makes Your Camera Roll Searchable, But It Can’t Tell Time’s Direction

Google’s new EmbeddingGemma 2 finds a clip among 40 videos from one sentence (13 of 14 searches hit #1). But play the same frames backwards and it barely notices: a video and its reverse are 99%+ similar. It sees what’s in a scene beautifully, and barely notices when.

See exactly where EmbeddingGemma 2 shines and where it fails, in the full video: https://t.co/91lSup2qGM

https://t.co/M4Hg1Yx6rC

selectedTweets.text:
Tiny embeddings connect words, images, audio, and video – and make me rethink what we need to remember.

Google released EmbeddingGemma 2, a model that can help you search videos with a spoken description, audio with a question, and images with a sketch - all on your device, with just 740M parameters.

Here is what makes this magic possible:

1. An embedding model makes information searchable by meaning. It turns content into numerical representations that place related things close together.

EmbeddingGemma 2 does this across modalities - that's why a question and a video clip become a match.
But a growing, searchable history has to fit somewhere.

2. The Matryoshka part helps with that:

A useful smaller representation sits inside the larger one. You can keep the first 256 numbers of a 768-number embedding, normalize it, and use it for search.

That means 1/3 of the vector storage, with ~95% of image, video, and speech retrieval quality, according to Google, making an index on your own device more practical.

Even something you barely remember seeing becomes something you might find again. Underneath agent memory is a deeper conversation about our own.

Read the full story on EmbeddingGemma 2, and why this memory conversation feels so personal ↓
